# Non-invasive estimation of skin thickness from hyperspectral imaging and validation using echography

  * Saurabh Vyas
  * , Jon Meyerle
  * , Philippe Burlina

  * School of Medicine

Research output: Contribution to journal › Article › peer-review

13   Link opens in a new tab Scopus citations

## Abstract

Background: The skin is the largest organ and is subject to the greatest exposure to outside elements throughout one[U+05F3]s lifetime. Current data by the American Academy of Dermatology suggests that approximately ten people die each hour worldwide due to skin related conditions. Cancers such as melanoma are growths that originate in the epidermis. Therefore, an accurate and non-invasive method to estimate skin constitutive elements can play an important clinical role in detecting the early onset of skin tumors. It can also serve as a valuable tool for research and development in cosmetics and pharmaceuticals in general.Methods: In our prior work, we developed a method that combined a physics-based model of human skin with machine learning and Hyperspectral imaging to non-invasively estimate physiological skin parameters, including melanosomes, collagen, oxygen saturation, and blood volume. In this work, we extend that model to also estimate skin thickness. Moreover, for the first time, we develop a protocol to test our methodology for skin thickness estimation using Ultrasound to acquire a gold standard dataset.Results: We tested our methodology for skin thickness estimation on a dataset of 48 Hyperspectral signatures obtained in vivo from six patients under IRB at Johns Hopkins Hospital. We found mean absolute errors on the order of the Ultrasound resolution (i.e., our gold standard).Discussion: This is the first study of its kind to validate skin thickness estimates using a gold standard. Our preliminary results constitute a proof-of-concept that hyperspectral-based methods can accurately and non-invasively estimate skin thickness in clinical settings.

## 2 Study area, model, and datasets

### 2.1 Study area

The TP, characterised by complex topography and highly heterogeneous climate and surface conditions, is one of the most prominent alpine regions globally. Influenced by both the Indian monsoon and mid-latitude westerlies, it exhibits a pronounced east-west gradient in climate and cryospheric conditions, supporting diverse hydrometeorological systems. As such, it serves as a key regulator of the Asian hydrological cycle (Bibi et al. Citation2018).

To address the computational challenges of complex sensitivity analysis, this study selects four representative upstream catchments along the southeast-northwest hydroclimatic gradient of the TP ([Button: Figure 1a–d], [Button: Table 1]). They are the upper Yarlung Zangbo River (UYZ) in the humid zone, the upper Yellow River (UYE) in the semi-humid zone, the upper Heihe River (UH) in the semi-arid zone, and the upper Yarkant River (UYA) in the arid zone.

This section introduces the methodological framework for assessing VIC model parameter sensitivity over the TP. The workflow integrates key parameter identification, analysis of environmental controls, and evaluation of modelling utility ([Button: Figure 2]). The experiment consists of four key components: parameter selection and sampling, model simulation and evaluation, global sensitivity analysis with environmental attribution, and parameter optimisation through case studies. Detailed procedures are provided in Sections 3.1–3.5.

### 3.1 Parameter selection and sampling

#### 3.1.1 Parameter range definition

We selected 33 representative parameters from the VIC model to capture key soil, vegetation, and snow processes ([Button: Table 2]), based on expert opinions, literature reviews, and recommendations from model developers. The parameter ranges were determined from their physical interpretation, model documentation, and relevant literature. Symmetric-LHS, an enhanced version of Latin Hypercube Sampling, improves sampling uniformity by ensuring symmetric and stratified distribution of samples across the parameter space (Ye, Li, and Sudjianto Citation2000; Gong et al. Citation2015). In this study, each parameter range was divided into 100 intervals using this strategy, generating 3,300 parameter sets for qualitative sensitivity analysis using MARs and DT. Saltelli sampling, specifically designed for variance-based global sensitivity analysis, constructs two base sample matrices and systematically combines them to efficiently calculate first-order and total-order sensitivity indices for all parameters (Saltelli et al. Citation2008). Following the Saltelli sampling scheme , where N denotes the base sample size (100) and D is the number of parameters (33 in this study), 3,500 samples per basin were generated for quantitative sensitivity analysis using the Sobol′ method.

#### 3.3.5 RF-SHAP framework for sensitivity attribution

The RF-SHAP algorithm (Deb and Smith Citation2021; He et al. Citation2023) was used to analyse the spatial variability of parameter sensitivity and its environmental drivers. The Random Forest algorithm was selected to construct the predictive model due to its strong resistance to overfitting and flexibility with data distribution, making it well-suited for multi-source heterogeneous data in hydrometeorology. The model uses parameter sensitivity scores from MARS, Delta Test, and Sobol’ as response variables, while climate factors (precipitation, temperature, wind speed, solar radiation, relative humidity, atmospheric and vapour pressure) and geographic attributes (elevation, latitude, longitude) serve as predictors. ## 4 Results

### 4.1 Parameter sensitivity analysis and drivers of spatial heterogeneity

This section explores the spatiotemporal sensitivity of hydrological model parameters in representative TP basins and the environmental factors driving spatial heterogeneity. First, we evaluated the consistency of results from Sobol′, MARS, and DT methods across various dimensions, confirming the necessity of a multi-method fusion strategy. Next, key sensitive parameters for nine hydrological variables were identified using KGE and SPAEF metrics, highlighting the dominant role of these parameters in snow-ice processes, energy balance, and runoff formation. Finally, the contributions of climate and surface factors to the spatial heterogeneity of parameter sensitivity were quantified using the RF-SHAP machine learning framework, offering insights into the underlying physical mechanisms.

#### 4.1.1 Consistency evaluation of multi-method sensitivity analysis

The consistency test results of the three sensitivity analysis methods, based on the top-k approach, showed strong agreement in identifying the top five sensitive parameters for most hydrological variables across various spatiotemporal scales. ## 6 Conclusions

This study developed a multi-scale parameter sensitivity analysis framework for cold-region hydrological modelling, focusing on four representative alpine basins along the hydroclimatic gradient of the Tibetan Plateau. The framework integrates nine hydro-energy outputs and systematically assesses parameter sensitivities across daily, spatial, and seasonal scales. By combining three global sensitivity methods (Sobol′, MARS, and DT) with two performance metrics (KGE and SPAEF), it captures the complex interactions between model parameters and outputs. The RF-SHAP approach is employed to identify key environmental drivers underlying spatial sensitivity variations. A comparison between runoff-only calibration and a multi-objective calibration, incorporating snow and energy processes, is also conducted. Additionally, a parameter transferability experiment, based on basin attribute similarity, assesses the transferability of parameter sensitivities.

The results indicate that snow albedo, leaf area index, and soil drainage parameters consistently exhibit high sensitivity across snow, energy, and water simulations. Incorporating prior hydrological knowledge in future studies will further enhance model calibration accuracy and physical consistency.

Global Sensitivity Analysis of an integrated parallel hydrologic model: ParFlow-CLM 

Wei Qu, Heye Bogena, Christoph Schüth, Harry Vereecken, and Stephan Schulz

An integrated parallel hydrologic model (ParFlow-CLM) was constructed to predict water and energy transport between subsurface, land surface, and atmosphere for a synthetic study using basic physical properties of the Stettbach headwater catchment, Germany. Based on this model, a global sensitivity analysis was performed using the Latin-Hypercube (LH) sampling strategy followed by the One-factor-At-a-Time (OAT) method to identify the most influential and interactive parameters affecting the main hydrologic processes. This study provides an efficient method of the identification of the most important input parameters of the model and how the variation in the output of a numerical model can be attributed to variations of its input factors. The results help to better understand process representation of the model and reduce the computational cost of running high numbers of simulations.

摘要: 电力系统在多个不可确定因素的影响下运行，这些因素无法确定地计算。分布预测被用于控制和减轻与此不确定性相关的风险。最近深度学习的进展显著提高了点预测的准确性，而准确的分布预测仍然是一个重大挑战。在本文中，我们提出了一种新颖的通用方法，用于进行分布预测，能够预测任意分位数。我们展示了我们的通用方法可以无缝地应用于两种不同的神经架构，从而在短期电力需求预测任务的背景下实现了最先进的分布预测结果。我们对35个欧洲国家的小时电力需求时间序列进行了实证验证。我们的代码可在此处找到：https://github.com/boreshkinai/any-quantile。

L33: Context 1
L34: ... sources, especially industrial, emit into the at- mosphere gases and aerosols, which play an important role in atmospheric exchanges. The use of new hyperspectral airborne sensors in the infrared range at high spatial resolution opens the way for further improvements in the characterization of industrial plumes.
L35: Existing methods, based on linear or Bayesian approach, present two major limitations: the heterogeneous environment impact on retrievals and the spatial and vertical extents of the plume are not considered. In this paper, a new method for plume characterization is presented to overcome such limitations. This method uses an accurate non linear formalism of cloud gas radiative impact.
L36: It includes furthermore a ground classification of the scene, in order to take into account the soil heterogeneity and spectral behaviour. This strategy will be validated using synthetic scenes of industrial area, and real data from Telops Hyper- Cam airborne platform. Index Terms — hyperspectral, plume, gas, thermal infrared, detection, characterization, Levenberg-Marquardt. Anthropogenic sources, especially industrial, are involved with a major contribution to air pollution.
L37: However, these emissions remain poorly estimated at a high spatial resolution. Recent technological advances in terms of spatial and spectral resolutions of thermal infrared airborne hyperspectral sensors, open a way of improving gaseous effluents characterization, since the majority of gas have their signatures in the thermal domain. In literature different approaches were proposed to quan- tify gaseous effluents using hyperspectral infrared imagery.
L38: Assuming plume gases are optically thin, Young [1] introduces a linear formalism to retrieve plume integrated column concentration of each pixel. A linear least-squares regression method is used to determine the thermal contrast, which is di- rectly related to the integrated column concentration. Heasler, et al. [2] follow a Bayesian approach. They developed a non-linear regression using the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm. The atmospheric terms are supposed to be known.
L39: As the background clutter (ground temperature and emissivity) is the dominant source of variability, it is handled as nui- sance parameters. A previous study [3] showed some of the limitations of such characterization methods. First, the spatial and vertical extents of the plume are not taken into account in these methods, which induces a miscalculation of the plume radiative impact. Then, the heterogeneous environment of an industrial scene impact a lot on the retrieval performances of these methods [4].
L40: Hereinafter, we present a new method of plume characterization, which takes into account the vertical extent of the plume. Moreover, our retrieval is preceded by a classification of the background, in order to deal with soil heterogeneity. The paper is organized in the following way: section 2 is ded- icated to the description of the plume retrieval methodology. Then, sections 3 and 4 evaluate the application of our method on synthetic data and Telops Hyper-Cam airborne platform data.
L41: Plume retrieval requires an accurate radiative model of the scene. To model the radiance at airborne sensor level, the following assumptions are done: 1) for each pixel, the ground is assumed to be homogeneous, flat and lambertian. 2) The plume is modeled as a set of flat layers, which are homogeneous in terms of temperature and gas concentrations. 3) The atmospheric profiles (pressure, temperature, water vapor, . . . ) are the same throughout the scene.
